reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Results from infarction of the ventral midbrain (cerebral peduncle) in the territory of paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral and basilar arteries
Defined by the combination of an ipsilateral oculomotor (third nerve) palsy with contralateral hemiparesis
The third nerve palsy produces a down-and-out eye, ptosis, and a dilated, poorly reactive pupil on the side of the lesion
Contralateral weakness affects the face, arm, and leg because the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres in the crus cerebri are damaged
It is the prototypical superior alternating hemiplegia and a form of crossed brainstem syndrome
The fascicle of the third nerve passes through the cerebral peduncle, explaining why a single lesion links the eye and limb signs
A pupil-involving third nerve palsy always demands exclusion of a compressive aneurysm before attributing it to brainstem ischaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Weber syndrome arises from ischaemia of the ventral (basal) midbrain, supplied by paramedian perforating branches of the posterior cerebral and top-of-basilar arteries. The lesion involves two adjacent structures: the emerging fascicles of the oculomotor nerve, giving an ipsilateral third nerve palsy with pupillary dilatation and ptosis, and the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres within the crus cerebri, giving contralateral weakness of the face and limbs. Because the descending motor fibres decussate more caudally, weakness is contralateral while the cranial nerve deficit is ipsilateral, producing the crossed pattern typical of alternating hemiplegias.
additionalDifferentials: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the third nerve
Uncal herniation with third nerve compression
Diabetic third nerve palsy (usually pupil-sparing and without hemiparesis)
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted MRI of the midbrain to confirm a paramedian peduncular infarct
MR or CT angiography of the posterior circulation and circle of Willis to exclude aneurysm
Formal assessment of pupillary size and reactivity to characterise the third nerve palsy
Cardiovascular and stroke risk workup including ECG and metabolic profiling
Vessel wall imaging where basilar atherosclerosis or dissection is considered
Blood glucose and inflammatory markers to weigh microvascular and inflammatory causes
redFlags: Pupil-involving third nerve palsy raising concern for a compressive posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Declining consciousness suggesting extension into the reticular activating system or top-of-basilar involvement
Bilateral signs indicating a larger paramedian midbrain or thalamic infarct
Rapid clinical deterioration implying evolving basilar occlusion
reference.prognosis: The oculomotor palsy and hemiparesis may partially improve with rehabilitation, but persistent diplopia, ptosis, and residual limb weakness are common, and outcome depends heavily on the underlying vascular cause.
pitfalls: Attributing a pupil-involving third nerve palsy to microvascular ischaemia without excluding an aneurysm
Missing the contralateral hemiparesis and treating the eye signs in isolation
Confusing Weber with tegmental midbrain syndromes that add tremor or ataxia
Overlooking evolving basilar territory ischaemia in a patient with only midbrain signs
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat as an acute posterior-circulation ischaemic stroke on the hyperacute pathway, offering intravenous thrombolysis and considering mechanical thrombectomy for eligible patients within the therapeutic window
Start secondary prevention with antiplatelet therapy, or anticoagulation if a cardioembolic source is confirmed
Reduce vascular risk with a statin, blood-pressure control, glycaemic management and smoking cessation
Refer for multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy and occupational therapy for the contralateral hemiparesis
Manage the oculomotor palsy and diplopia with temporary occlusion or prisms, reserving strabismus surgery for stable residual deviation
Exclude an aneurysm or basilar dissection as the cause, and escalate urgently for fluctuating brainstem signs suggesting evolving basilar occlusion
